orig_9709_s1_ct_centre_raw.description: Calculate each centre from the information it uses, keep every tied mode, and choose a summary that answers the question. Distinguish a raw mode from a grouped modal class and support mixed questions with a short spread application.

sections.title: How do I calculate a mean or recover a total?
sections.label: Every value contributes
sections.intro:
The mean, median and mode describe different aspects of a dataset’s centre. Name the measure you use instead of writing only “average”. For \(n\ge1\) numerical observations, the arithmetic mean is

\[\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x_i}{n}=\frac{T}{n}.\]

The symbol \(\sum\) means add the values. Count every recorded observation, including repeats and zeros.

blocks.html:
\[T=n\bar{x}.\]

Use this reverse relationship when a mean and count are given. If a record is added or removed, update both the total and the count. If an existing record is corrected, subtract the wrong value and add its replacement; the count stays unchanged.

blocks.title: Recover a missing observation from the mean
blocks.prompt: Five completion times, in seconds, are \(8,9,11,12,x\). Their mean is exactly \(11\) seconds. Find their total and the missing time \(x\).
blocks.hint: Reverse the mean formula: total equals count multiplied by mean. Then subtract every known observation.
blocks.solution:
1. \[T=5(11)=55\,\mathrm{s}.\]
  2. \[8+9+11+12=40,\qquad x=55-40=15\,\mathrm{s}.\]

  3. The completed list totals \(55\) seconds, so its mean is \(\frac{55}{5}=11\) seconds.

blocks.html: A mean need not be an observed value and can be fractional even for integer counts. Check that it lies between the smallest and largest records, and keep full intermediate totals before rounding.

sections.title: How do I find the median?
sections.label: Order first, then select positions
sections.intro: The median is determined by ordered positions, so put the complete list in increasing order first. Repeated values remain separate observations.

blocks.html:
For an odd count, take the observation in position \(\frac{n+1}{2}\). For an even count, average the values in positions \(\frac{n}{2}\) and \(\frac{n}{2}+1\).

The positions identify which records to use; the median is their value or their arithmetic mean.

blocks.title: Order before choosing the middle
blocks.prompt:
Two recorded-time samples, in seconds, are

\[A:\quad17,4,11,8,8,14;\qquad B:\quad5,13,7,7,11.\]

Find the median of each sample.
blocks.hint: Put each list in increasing order. A has two middle positions; B has one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[A:\quad4,8,8,11,14,17.\]

    The third and fourth observations are \(8\) and \(11\), so

    \[M_A=\frac{8+11}{2}=\frac{19}{2}\,\mathrm{s}.\]
  2. \[B:\quad5,7,7,11,13.\]

    The third observation is the median: \(M_B=7\,\mathrm{s}\).

blocks.html: Do not take the middle item of an unordered list. For an even count, average the two middle values, not their position numbers or the smallest and largest values.

sections.title: What counts as a mode or a modal class?
sections.label: Raw frequencies and grouped densities
sections.intro: For raw values or named categories, count how often each occurs. Every value tied for the greatest frequency is a mode when that greatest frequency exceeds one. Two tied modes are called bimodal.

blocks.html: Raw-data convention in this course: if every value occurs once, report no mode. Otherwise retain every value tied at the greatest frequency; do not choose only the smallest, largest or first one.

Grouped convention in this course: for unequal-width numerical classes, a modal class has the greatest frequency density, so it is a tallest histogram bar:

\[d=\frac{f}{\text{class width}}.\]

This is different from simply finding the class with greatest frequency. Some tables or questions define “modal class” by greatest frequency; follow an explicit definition. When all widths are equal, the two rankings agree.
The middle class has greatest density \(3\) and is the modal class under this course’s convention. The last class has greatest frequency \(24\).

blocks.title: Report every tied mode and distinguish a modal class
blocks.prompt:
Find all modes of \(2,3,3,5,5,8\). Also state the mode result for \(1,6,10,12\), using this course’s convention that an all-unique list has no mode.

A separate grouped dataset has the classes below. Using the course convention that modal classes have greatest frequency density, give every modal class number and the class number with greatest frequency.

Class numberIntervalFrequency
\(1\)\(0\le x<2\)\(8\)
\(2\)\(2\le x<6\)\(16\)
\(3\)\(6\le x<12\)\(12\)

fields.label: All modes of the repeated-value list
Mode result for the all-unique list
All modal class numbers under the stated convention

blocks.hint: Count occurrences for raw modes. For the grouped table, calculate each width and divide its frequency by that width.
blocks.solution:
1. Both \(3\) and \(5\) occur twice, while the other listed values occur once. The two modes are \(3\) and \(5\).

  2. Every value in \(1,6,10,12\) occurs once, so the result is no mode under the stated convention.

  3. \[d_1=\frac{8}{2}=4,\qquad d_2=\frac{16}{4}=4,\qquad d_3=\frac{12}{6}=2.\]

  4. Classes \(1\) and \(2\) tie for greatest density, so retain both as modal classes. Class \(2\) alone has greatest frequency, \(16\).

blocks.html: Retain all classes tied at the greatest density. If every class has the same density, say there is no unique modal class. A grouped modal interval does not identify an exact raw-data modal value.

sections.title: Which measure answers the question best?
sections.label: Typical values, totals and categories
sections.intro: Choose the centre for the purpose, not just because it is easiest to calculate. The mean uses every magnitude and connects directly to a total. The median uses positions and is less sensitive to the size of an existing extreme observation. The mode identifies the most common value or category.

blocks.html:
PurposeUseful centreReason
Recover a total or describe an equal shareMeanCount multiplied by mean gives the total.
Describe a typical numerical value when a few magnitudes are extremeMedianThe ordered middle is less influenced by how far an extreme value lies.
Identify the most popular named categoryModeCategory frequencies are meaningful; averaging nominal labels is not.
Replacing the existing largest time \(16\) by \(58\) changes the mean from \(10\) to \(16\) seconds, while the median and mode remain \(10\) in this example.

blocks.title: Choose a centre for the question being asked
blocks.prompt:
Seven completion times, in seconds, are

\[3,4,5,5,6,7,40.\]

Calculate the mean and median. Choose a measure to describe a typical completion time without the single very long time dominating the result. Then choose the measure that, multiplied by seven, recovers the exact total duration of these recorded tasks.

fields.label: Measure suited to the stated typical-time purpose
Measure that recovers the total when multiplied by seven

blocks.hint: The ordered middle is the fourth observation. The mean uses every value and is linked directly to the total.
blocks.solution:
1. \[T=3+4+5+5+6+7+40=70,\qquad\bar{t}=\frac{70}{7}=10\,\mathrm{s}.\]

  2. The fourth observation gives median \(5\,\mathrm{s}\). It is the suitable measure for the stated typical-time description.

  3. The exact total is \(7\bar{t}=7(10)=70\,\mathrm{s}\). Multiplying the median or mode by seven would give \(35\), which is not the total. The long recorded time still contributes to the work actually completed.

blocks.html: “Less sensitive” does not mean “never changes”. Adding or removing a record changes the count and may move the median positions; moving a value across the middle may also change the median. An unusual record is not automatically an error. For nominal categories, numerical codes are labels, so their mean or median is not a meaningful centre.

sections.title: How do mixed questions add spread to the mean?
sections.label: Application: descriptive variance and SD
sections.intro:
Extension bridge: later lessons develop measures of variation in detail. This short application supplies the formulas needed when a question asks for both a centre and a measure of spread.

Descriptive variance is the average squared distance from the mean, using the number of observations \(n\) as divisor. Standard deviation is its square root.

blocks.html:
\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n}=\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2},\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

Variance has squared measurement units; standard deviation has the original units. Two datasets can have the same mean and different spread.

blocks.title: Application: add a descriptive measure of spread
blocks.prompt: Application after the centre methods: four masses, in grams, are \(1,3,5,7\). Find the mean, descriptive variance using divisor \(n=4\), and standard deviation. Give exact answers.
blocks.hint: Calculate both the total and the sum of squares. Use \(\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2}\), then take a square root for standard deviation.

blocks.html: These descriptive questions use divisor \(n\). If using a calculator, choose the corresponding population/descriptive standard deviation rather than a result based on \(n-1\). Distinguish \(\sum x_i^2\), the sum of squares, from \((\sum x_i)^2\), the square of the total. Square a supplied standard deviation only when variance is needed.

glossary.definition: The total of every numerical observation divided by the number of observations.
The middle of an ordered list, averaging the two middle values for an even count.
A value or category with greatest frequency; this course reports no mode when every value occurs once.
Having exactly two modes, both tied at the greatest frequency.
Here, a grouped class with greatest frequency density; follow an explicit different definition when a question supplies one.
The class frequency divided by its width, \(d=\frac{f}{w}\).
A category label without a meaningful numerical order or measurement scale.
The mean squared distance from the data mean, using the record count \(n\) as divisor.
The square root of variance, in the original measurement units.

examples.title: Use every observation and the correct count
examples.question: Seven completion times, in seconds, are \(6,\ 8,\ 9,\ 10,\ 10,\ 11,\ 16\). Find their mean. An eighth time of \(18\) seconds is then recorded; find the new mean.
solution:
Add every observation, including both occurrences of \(10\):

\[T=6+8+9+10+10+11+16=70\,\mathrm{s}.\]

After adding the new record, both the total and the count change:

\[T_{\mathrm{new}}=70+18=88,\qquad n_{\mathrm{new}}=8.\]

\[\bar{t}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{88}{8}=11\,\mathrm{s}.\]

The added time exceeds the old mean, so an increased mean is sensible.

examples.title: Find the median of an unordered even sample
examples.question: Eight times, in seconds, are \(15,7,12,9,11,9,18,13\). Find the median.
solution:
Keep both occurrences of \(9\) and order the records:

\[7,9,9,11,12,13,15,18.\]
With \(n=8\), the middle positions are \(\frac{8}{2}=4\) and \(5\). Their values are \(11\) and \(12\).

\[M=\frac{11+12}{2}=\frac{23}{2}=11.5\,\mathrm{s}.\]

The median need not be an observed value when the count is even.

examples.title: Keep tied modes and recognise no mode
examples.question:
Find the modes of these two numerical lists:

\[A:\quad4,4,6,9,9,12;\qquad B:\quad2,5,8,11.\]

Use the course’s no-mode convention for an all-unique list. A separate colour survey records blue \(7\), green \(4\) and red \(7\) responses. Identify its modal categories.
solution:
In A, \(4\) and \(9\) each occur twice; \(6\) and \(12\) each occur once. The greatest frequency is \(2\), so the modes are

\[\{4,9\}.\]
In B, every value occurs once. Under the stated convention, there is no mode.
The colour survey has two categories tied at frequency \(7\): blue and red. A mode can describe a category even when adding or averaging the category labels has no meaning.

examples.title: Use density for this course’s unequal-width modal class
examples.question:
A separate sample of \(50\) completion times is grouped as follows.

Time \(t\), in secondsFrequency
\(0\le t<4\)\(8\)
\(4\le t<10\)\(18\)
\(10\le t<22\)\(24\)

Using the course’s greatest-density convention, find the modal class. Also identify the class with greatest frequency.
solution:
The widths are \(4\), \(6\) and \(12\) seconds. Calculate density separately for each class:

\[d_1=\frac{8}{4}=2,\qquad d_2=\frac{18}{6}=3,\qquad d_3=\frac{24}{12}=2.\]

The greatest density is \(3\), so the modal class under this convention is

\[4\le t<10.\]
The greatest frequency is \(24\), in \(10\le t<22\). Its larger width explains why it can contain more observations without having the tallest histogram bar.
The grouped table identifies a modal interval under the stated rule. It does not reveal an exact modal time among the original records.

examples.title: Let the purpose decide between mean and median
examples.question: The recorded times \(6,\ 8,\ 9,\ 10,\ 10,\ 11,\ 16\) seconds have mean, median and mode all equal to \(10\). Replace the existing \(16\)-second record by \(58\) seconds, keeping seven records. Recalculate the three centres, then choose a summary for a typical time and a summary that preserves the total.
solution: \[T_{\mathrm{new}}=70-16+58=112\,\mathrm{s},\qquad\bar{t}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{112}{7}=16\,\mathrm{s}.\]
The new ordered list is \(6,8,9,10,10,11,58\). Its fourth value is still \(10\), and \(10\) is still the only repeated value. The median and mode remain \(10\,\mathrm{s}\).
For a typical time that is less influenced by this extreme magnitude, report the median \(10\,\mathrm{s}\). Explain why the mean is higher rather than silently dropping the long record.

To describe the exact total or an equal share of that total, the mean is appropriate:

\[7(16)=112\,\mathrm{s}.\]

The two centres answer different questions. This replacement left the middle position unchanged; adding or removing a record could change it.

examples.title: Application: measure spread around a known mean
examples.question: Application: three heights are \(2,5,8\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find their mean, descriptive variance using divisor \(3\), and standard deviation.
solution:
The deviations from the mean are \(-3,0,3\). Squaring prevents their signs from cancelling:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{(-3)^2+0^2+3^2}{3}=6\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

The sum-of-squares formula gives the same result:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{2^2+5^2+8^2}{3}-5^2=\frac{93}{3}-25=6\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

\[\sigma=\sqrt{6}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Standard deviation has the original measurement units; variance has squared units.

extraPractice.title: Three centres need not agree
extraPractice.prompt:
Signed measurement errors, in centimetres, are

\[-6,-2,-2,0,3,7.\]

Find the exact mean, median and every mode.
extraPractice.hint: Keep the negative signs in the total. The six ordered observations have two middle positions, not one.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sum x=-6-2-2+0+3+7=0,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{0}{6}=0\ \text{cm}.\]
  2. \[M=\frac{-2+0}{2}=-1\ \text{cm}.\]

  3. The value \(-2\) cm occurs twice; every other value occurs once. The only mode is \(-2\) cm. A mean of zero does not imply that all errors are zero.

extraPractice.title: Retain all tied modes and recognise the no-mode case
extraPractice.prompt:
Give every mode for each dataset.

\[A:1,1,3,3,5,5,8;\qquad B:2,4,6,9.\]

Use this chapter’s convention: if every value occurs once, there is no mode; otherwise give every value tied for greatest frequency. You may type “no mode”.
extraPractice.hint: Count the frequency of each distinct value. A tie at the greatest repeated frequency is not the same as a list with no repeats.
extraPractice.solution:
1. For A, each of \(1,3,5\) occurs twice, while \(8\) occurs once. Its complete modal set is \(\{1,3,5\}\).

  2. For B, all four distinct values occur once. Under the stated convention, B has no mode.

extraPractice.title: An extreme observation affects different summaries differently
extraPractice.prompt: Five repair costs, in pounds, are \(10,12,14,14,70\). The cost \(70\) is then corrected to \(170\). Find the original mean, corrected mean and corrected median. Which measure, multiplied by the count of five, recovers the total corrected cost exactly?

fields.label: Measure that recovers the total when multiplied by five

extraPractice.hint: The total rises by the change in the corrected value. Check whether its position crosses either central observation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T=10+12+14+14+70=120,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{120}{5}=\text{£}24.\]
  2. \[T_{\rm corrected}=120-70+170=220,\qquad\bar{x}_{\rm corrected}=\frac{220}{5}=\text{£}44.\]

  3. The ordered corrected data are \(10,12,14,14,170\). The median remains \(\text{£}14\), and the mode also remains \(\text{£}14\).

  4. The mean rises by \(\text{£}20\), while the median is unchanged because the middle position is unchanged. The corrected mean still satisfies \(5\times44=220\); an extreme value does not make the mean useless when the total is the question.

extraPractice.title: State the modal-class convention when widths differ
extraPractice.prompt:
The grouped continuous data have:

Class numberIntervalFrequency
\(1\)\(0\le x<2\)6
\(2\)\(2\le x<8\)12
\(3\)\(8\le x<12\)12

In this course, a modal class is a class with greatest frequency density. Give every modal class number, then every class number with greatest frequency.
extraPractice.hint: The widths are \(2,6,4\). Divide each frequency by its own width before identifying the density peaks.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[d_1=\frac{6}{2}=3,\qquad d_2=\frac{12}{6}=2,\qquad d_3=\frac{12}{4}=3.\]

  2. Classes \(1\) and \(3\) tie for greatest density, so both are modal classes under the stated convention. Classes \(2\) and \(3\) tie for greatest frequency, \(12\).

  3. With unequal widths, “greatest frequency” and “greatest frequency density” can give different answers. A grouped modal class does not identify an exact raw modal value within it.

extraPractice.title: Mixed application: equal centres can hide different spreads
extraPractice.prompt:
Mixed application — descriptive variance and standard deviation. Two sets of lengths, in centimetres, are

\[A:7,8,9;\qquad B:2,8,14.\]

Both means are \(8\) cm. Using divisor \(n=3\), find the variance and standard deviation of each sample. Which has the more tightly grouped observations?
extraPractice.hint: Calculate the average squared distance from the mean. Then take the square root to obtain the standard deviation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sigma_A^2=\frac{(7-8)^2+(8-8)^2+(9-8)^2}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  2. \[\sigma_A=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\ \text{cm}.\]
  3. \[\sigma_B^2=\frac{(2-8)^2+(8-8)^2+(14-8)^2}{3}=24\ \text{cm}^{2},\quad\sigma_B=2\sqrt{6}\ \text{cm}.\]

  4. A has less spread despite the equal means. Variance uses squared units; standard deviation uses the original length unit.

starters.title: Different questions can favour different centres
starters.question:
Recorded delivery times, in minutes, are

\[A:8,9,10,10,11,12,50;\]\[B:12,13,14,14,15,16,17.\]

Find each exact mean and median. Which sample has the lower typical time by the median? Which has the lower total recorded time across its seven deliveries? Explain why these conclusions can differ.
starters.hint: Keep the total for each sample as well as its mean. The long A delivery changes its total without changing the middle observation.
starters.solution:
1. \[T_A=110,\quad T_B=101,\quad\bar{x}_A=\frac{110}{7},\quad\bar{x}_B=\frac{101}{7}\ \text{min}.\]

  2. Both lists are ordered and contain seven times. Their medians are the fourth observations: \(10\) min for A and \(14\) min for B.

  3. A has the lower typical time by the median. B has the lower observed total, \(101\) min rather than \(110\) min, and therefore the lower mean for these equal sample sizes.

  4. A’s long \(50\)-minute delivery raises its mean. The median can describe a typical delivery with less sensitivity to that value; the total and mean answer the different question of how much time the recorded deliveries consumed altogether.

  5. Neither conclusion establishes which method will be faster on every future delivery, and the long record should not be discarded merely because it changes the mean.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain both sample counts and totals.
  • 1 mark: obtain the exact mean of A.
  • 1 mark: obtain the exact mean of B.
  • 1 mark: locate both ordered median positions.
  • 1 mark: obtain both medians.
  • 1 mark: identify the lower typical time by the median.
  • 1 mark: identify the lower total and relate it to the mean.
  • 1 mark: explain the difference in purpose and the effect of the extreme observation.

starters.title: Use a measure that makes sense for categories
starters.question:
Students reported their usual travel method. Each student selected exactly one category.

CategoryFrequency
Bus12
Walking9
Cycling12
Car3

Find the total number of students, identify every modal category, and find the fraction using one of those modal categories. A spreadsheet labels the categories with the numerical codes \(1,2,3,4\). Does the mean of those codes give a meaningful average travel method?
starters.hint: The modal categories tie at the greatest frequency. Distinguish numerical measurements from numbers used only as labels.
starters.solution:
1. \[N=12+9+12+3=36.\]

  2. Bus and cycling each occur \(12\) times, the greatest frequency. Both are modes.

  3. \[\text{fraction in the modal categories}=\frac{12+12}{36}=\frac{2}{3}.\]

  4. The category codes have no measurement scale or natural order. Relabelling the same categories would change their arithmetic mean without changing anybody’s travel method. The modes provide a meaningful description of the most common categories.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: sum all category frequencies.
  • 1 mark: identify both tied modal categories.
  • 1 mark: add the frequencies of both modal categories.
  • 1 mark: obtain the fraction of the full sample.
  • 1 mark: explain why the arbitrary category codes do not support a meaningful mean.

revision.body:
Calculate the requested centre, state all tied modes, and justify the choice using the purpose of the question.

Mean and median use different information

\[\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x}{n},\qquad\sum x=n\bar{x}.\]

The mean uses every numerical observation. For the median, order all values and keep repeats. For odd \(n\), take position \(\frac{n+1}{2}\). For even \(n\), average the two middle values. Positions are not the answer values.

State every mode and the grouped convention

The mode is a most frequent observed value. If the greatest frequency exceeds one, include every tied value. If every value occurs once, this chapter uses “no mode”.

For grouped continuous data, this course defines modal classes by greatest density \(d=\frac{f}{w}\). Unequal widths can make the greatest-frequency class different. Retain all density ties; equal densities give no unique modal class. Grouping does not reveal an exact modal raw value.

Choose the centre for the question

The median is less sensitive to the size of an extreme value; the mean recovers the total when multiplied by the count. The mode describes the most common category. Numerical category codes do not create a meaningful measurement mean.

Explain the purpose and quote units. A higher centre is not universally better, and an outlier does not automatically invalidate the mean.

Mixed application: centre does not determine spread

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^2}{n}=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2},\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

Here descriptive variance uses divisor \(n\). Standard deviation uses the original units; variance uses squared units. Equal means need not imply equal consistency. This bridge supports mixed questions; the variation chapter develops it further.
revision.checks:
• Every observation included in the total and count?
  • Median positions found after ordering?
  • Every tied mode and the stated class convention used?
  • Choice explained in context, with spread considered separately?
