revision.body:
Combine two disjoint datasets through their counts and compatible moment totals, then calculate the required summaries.

Recover totals before averaging groups

\[N=n_A+n_B,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{n_A\bar{x}_A+n_B\bar{x}_B}{N}.\]

Each observation receives equal weight, so each group mean is weighted by its count. For two positive counts and different means, the combined mean lies strictly between them. An unweighted average agrees when counts are equal or the group means coincide.

Add both moment totals

\[T_i=n_i\bar{x}_i,\qquad Q_i=n_i(\sigma_i^2+\bar{x}_i^{\,2}).\]\[\bar{x}=\frac{T_A+T_B}{N},\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{Q_A+Q_B}{N}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

Use descriptive variance with divisor equal to the group count. Reconstruct a square-sum using variance, not SD. Take the square root only after finding the combined variance. Subtract counts and both totals to recover a hidden group.

Two sources contribute to pooled spread

\[\sigma^2=\frac{n_A\sigma_A^2+n_B\sigma_B^2}{N}+\frac{n_An_B}{N^2}(\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B)^2.\]

The first term describes spread within groups. The second describes separation of their centres. Even two constant groups can have positive pooled variance. Averaging SDs is not a general pooling rule. Pooling records is different from adding random variables.

Restore units and check reverse problems

Decode each group separately and convert both to the same measurement units before adding totals. Under a scale factor \(c\), SD changes by \(|c|\) and variance by \(c^2\).

For an unknown group count, keep it in both the weighted total and the total count. Check the target mean, integer and positivity conditions, and the original equation. Equal group means may leave the count undetermined. Summary moments alone generally do not reveal a pooled median or mode.
revision.checks:
• Same quantity and units; each record counted once?
  • Both counts and both moment totals combined?
  • Between-group separation included in the variance?
  • Unknown counts and recovered summaries checked?

orig_9709_s1_ct_changes.description: Identify exactly which records changed, then update the count, total and sum of squares. Use those quantities to correct summaries, recover missing values and test every allowed solution.

sections.title: How do I correct one recorded value?
sections.label: Replace a record
sections.intro:
Keep track of three quantities: the number of observations \(n\), the total \(T=\sum x\), and the sum of squares \(Q=\sum x^2\). For a nonempty dataset,

\[\mu=\frac{T}{n},\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{Q}{n}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

All variances here are descriptive, using the full count as the divisor. If only summaries are given, restore \(T=n\mu\) and \(Q=n(\sigma^2+\mu^2)\).

Replacing an incorrect value \(a\) by its correct value \(b\) keeps the same record:

\[n_{\mathrm{new}}=n,\qquad T_{\mathrm{new}}=T-a+b,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{new}}=Q-a^2+b^2.\]

blocks.html: The sum-of-squares change is \(b^2-a^2\), not \((b-a)^2\). Recalculate variance using the corrected mean as well as the corrected sum of squares.
Replacing \(9\) by \(13\) changes the total by \(4\), the sum of squares by \(88\), and leaves the count unchanged.

blocks.title: Replace a value without adding a record
blocks.prompt: Six numerical records have mean \(10\) and descriptive variance \(9\). One recorded value \(12\) should be \(6\). Find the corrected count, sum of squares, mean and variance.
blocks.hint: Recover the old total and sum of squares first. Replace the contribution of the wrong value in both totals, keeping the count unchanged.

blocks.html:
The change in mean also gives

\[b-a=n(\mu_{\mathrm{new}}-\mu).\]

This can recover an unknown count, which must be a positive integer. If the mean change is zero, check the equation directly before dividing; a genuine one-value correction with \(a\ne b\) cannot leave the mean unchanged.

sections.title: What changes when a record is added or removed?
sections.label: Add, remove, deduplicate
sections.intro:
Adding a new observation or removing an existing one changes the number of records:

OperationNew countNew totalNew sum of squares
Add a new value \(b\)\(n+1\)\(T+b\)\(Q+b^2\)
Remove one value \(a\)\(n-1\)\(T-a\)\(Q-a^2\)

Use the new count in both the mean and variance. After removal, at least one observation must remain for these summaries to exist. A one-observation dataset has variance zero; an empty dataset has no mean or variance.

blocks.html: An erroneous duplicate means one record was entered an extra time: remove only the extra copy. Separate genuine records can have equal values, so equal values alone do not justify deletion.

blocks.title: Remove only the extra copy
blocks.prompt: Five recorded observations have \(T=35\) and \(Q=315\). One value \(7\) was entered twice by mistake, and exactly one extra copy must be deleted. Find the corrected count, mean and descriptive variance. Separately, would a mean and variance exist if the only observation in a dataset were removed?

fields.label: Mean and variance after removing the only observation

options.undefined: Both are undefined because no observations remain.

blocks.hint: A deletion changes the count as well as both totals. Remove one contribution of \(7\), not every occurrence of that value.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n_{\mathrm{new}}=4,\qquad T_{\mathrm{new}}=35-7=28,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{new}}=315-7^2=266.\]
  2. \[\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{28}{4}=7,\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{266}{4}-7^2=\frac{35}{2}.\]

  3. Removing the sole observation leaves count \(0\). The formulas would divide by zero, so the empty dataset has no mean or descriptive variance.

blocks.html: For a new median, sort the updated raw records and locate their new central positions. For a new mode, recount the frequencies. Counts and moment totals alone generally do not determine those summaries.

sections.title: Can the mean stay unchanged while SD changes?
sections.label: Unchanged mean
sections.intro:
Adding a value equal to the current mean leaves that mean unchanged. The added squared deviation is zero, but there is one more record to share the existing squared deviations:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{n}{n+1}\sigma^2.\]

If the original variance is positive, it decreases; if all original observations are equal, it remains zero. Similarly, removing an existing observation equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged and gives

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{n}{n-1}\sigma^2,\qquad n>1.\]

The divisor change matters even when the centre does not move.

blocks.title: Keep the mean but change the spread
blocks.prompt: The observations are \(1,3,5,7\). Add a fifth observation equal to their original mean. Find the new mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation.
blocks.hint: The old mean is \(4\). The added value contributes zero squared deviation from that same mean, but the divisor increases.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=4,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{1^2+3^2+5^2+7^2}{4}-4^2=5.\]

  2. Add the value \(4\). The mean remains \(4\), while

    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{4}{5}(5)=4,\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}=2.\]

  3. The original SD was \(\sqrt{5}\). An unchanged mean has not kept the SD unchanged.

sections.title: How do two missing observations come from mean and variance?
sections.label: Recover missing values
sections.intro:
First recover the full \(T\) and \(Q\). Subtract the known records and their squares separately. If the remaining information is

\[p+q=S,\qquad p^2+q^2=R,\]

then

\[pq=\frac{S^2-R}{2}.\]

Each missing value is a root of

\[z^2-Sz+\frac{S^2-R}{2}=0.\]

blocks.html:
Check that real missing values can exist:

\[(p-q)^2=2R-S^2\ge0.\]

A negative result means no real pair; zero gives equal values. A positive result gives two values, and both labelled assignments remain possible unless an order or context restriction selects one. A positive proposed overall variance alone is not sufficient.

blocks.title: Recover the labelled pair and reject impossible moments
blocks.prompt: Four numerical observations are \(0,6,p,q\). Their mean is \(5\), and their descriptive variance is \(13\). Find every labelled pair \((p,q)\). A separate proposal gives the same known records and mean but variance \(8\). Could that proposal have real missing observations?

fields.label: Can the separate variance proposal be realised?

options.no: No: it would require a negative squared difference.
options.yes: Yes: any positive overall variance is feasible.
options.equal: Yes: it forces the two missing values to be equal.

blocks.hint: Restore the full total and sum of squares, then subtract the known contributions. The missing sum and sum of squares must also be compatible with real values.
blocks.solution:
1. \[p+q=4(5)-0-6=14.\]\[p^2+q^2=4(13+5^2)-0^2-6^2=116.\]
  2. \[pq=\frac{14^2-116}{2}=40,\qquad z^2-14z+40=(z-4)(z-10)=0.\]
  3. \[(p,q)=(4,10)\text{ or }(10,4).\]

    Either pair gives total \(20\), sum of squares \(152\), mean \(5\) and variance \(13\).

  4. For the separate variance \(8\), the missing sum of squares would be

    \[R=4(8+25)-36=96.\]\[(p-q)^2=2R-(p+q)^2=192-196=-4.\]

    A real square cannot be negative, so there is no real pair.

blocks.html: The mean alone usually determines only the missing sum. Keep every valid branch, then check the original mean, variance and any restrictions such as non-negative, integer, distinct or ordered observations.

sections.title: Which added values satisfy a variance limit?
sections.label: Variance as a quadratic
sections.intro:
This application uses completing the square and quadratic inequalities. If one real value \(t\) is added to \(n\) original observations, start with

\[V(t)=\frac{Q+t^2}{n+1}-\left(\frac{T+t}{n+1}\right)^2.\]

Expanding and completing the square gives a quadratic you can solve without differentiation. Equivalently, if the original mean is \(\mu\) and variance is \(\sigma^2\),

\[V(t)=\frac{n}{n+1}\sigma^2+\frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(t-\mu)^2.\]

Its minimum occurs at \(t=\mu\), with value \(\frac{n}{n+1}\sigma^2\). This minimum is positive unless all the original records are equal.

blocks.html: For original observations \(1,4,7\), the variance is \(V(t)=\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{16}(t-4)^2\). The bound \(V(t)\le6\) keeps the whole interval between \(4-2\sqrt{2}\) and \(4+2\sqrt{2}\).

blocks.title: Find the real interval, then apply the count restriction
blocks.prompt: Two observed counts are \(0\) and \(4\). A third count \(t\) is added. First treat \(t\) as real and find the lower and upper endpoints of the complete interval on which the new descriptive variance is at most \(4\). Then list all allowed values when \(t\) must be a non-negative integer.

fields.label: Lower endpoint of the unrestricted real interval
Upper endpoint of the unrestricted real interval

blocks.hint: There are three records after adding \(t\). Express the variance in terms of \(t\), complete the square and retain both bounds before applying the original count restriction.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n_{\mathrm{new}}=3,\qquad T=4+t,\qquad Q=16+t^2.\]\[V(t)=\frac{16+t^2}{3}-\left(\frac{4+t}{3}\right)^2=\frac{8}{3}+\frac{2}{9}(t-2)^2.\]
  2. \[V(t)\le4\Longleftrightarrow\frac{2}{9}(t-2)^2\le\frac{4}{3}\Longleftrightarrow(t-2)^2\le6.\]
  3. \[2-\sqrt{6}\le t\le2+\sqrt{6}.\]

    Both endpoints are included because the variance is allowed to equal \(4\).

  4. Since \(2\lt \sqrt{6}\lt 3\), the real interval begins between \(-1\) and \(0\) and ends between \(4\) and \(5\). Its non-negative integers are

    \[t\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}.\]

blocks.html: For a non-strict upper bound \(V(t)\le c\), subtract the minimum and isolate the square. A bound below the minimum gives no solutions; a bound equal to the minimum gives one value. For a larger bound, retain both endpoints and every value between them. For the strict condition \(V(t)\lt c\), a bound equal to the minimum gives no solutions; a larger bound excludes its boundary values. An exact target above the minimum has two real solutions before any context restrictions are applied.

glossary.definition: Changing the value in one existing record. The number of records stays the same.
Adding a new observation, increasing the count by one.
Removing one existing observation, decreasing the count by one.
An extra entry of the same record, as distinct from two genuine records that happen to have equal values.
The total \(Q=\sum x^2\), obtained by squaring individual observations before adding.
The average squared deviation of the given records from their mean, using their actual count as divisor.
An assignment such as \((p,q)\), where swapping the two values changes the assignment unless the values are equal.
Values that satisfy both original moment equations and all stated restrictions.
A constant plus a positive multiple of a square, showing the minimum of the variance model.
An additional requirement such as non-negative, integer, distinct or ordered observations.

examples.title: Correct both totals
examples.question: The four recorded observations are \(3,5,7,9\). The final value should be \(13\), not \(9\). Find the corrected mean and descriptive variance.
solution:
The correction replaces one record, so the count stays \(4\):

\[T_{\mathrm{new}}=24-9+13=28,\]\[Q_{\mathrm{new}}=164-9^2+13^2=252.\]
\[\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{28}{4}=7,\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{252}{4}-7^2=14.\]
Directly checking the corrected list \(3,5,7,13\) gives those same totals. The sum of squares increased by \(13^2-9^2=88\), not by \((13-9)^2=16\).

examples.title: Delete one erroneous duplicate
examples.question: The recorded list is \(2,5,5,8,10\). One of the two entries \(5\) is an extra copy of the same record. Remove exactly one copy, then find the corrected mean, median and descriptive variance.
solution: \[n_{\mathrm{new}}=4,\qquad T_{\mathrm{new}}=30-5=25,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{new}}=218-5^2=193.\]
\[\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{25}{4},\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{193}{4}-\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)^2=\frac{147}{16}.\]

The corrected ordered list is \(2,5,8,10\). Its two middle values are \(5\) and \(8\), so

\[\text{median}=\frac{5+8}{2}=\frac{13}{2}.\]

The valid remaining record \(5\) is retained.

examples.title: Insert the mean and update the divisor
examples.question: The three observations are \(1,4,7\). Add a fourth observation equal to their mean. Compare the original and new means and descriptive variances.
solution: The added value is \(4\), so the new total is \(16\) and the new count is \(4\). The mean remains \(4\).

The added value has zero deviation from that mean. The squared deviations still total \(18\), but now

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{18}{4}=\frac{9}{2}=\frac{3}{4}(6).\]
The mean is unchanged while the positive variance decreases. The SD changes from \(\sqrt{6}\) to \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\).

examples.title: Find both missing values from two moments
examples.question: The five observations are \(2,4,8,p,q\). Their mean is \(6\), and their descriptive variance is \(8\). Find all labelled pairs \((p,q)\). Then state which pair satisfies \(p\lt q\).
solution:
The missing observations are the roots of

\[z^2-16z+60=(z-6)(z-10)=0.\]

Thus the labelled pairs are \((6,10)\) and \((10,6)\). The condition \(p\lt q\) selects \((6,10)\).
Either labelled assignment gives total \(30\) and sum of squares \(220\). Hence the original mean is \(6\) and variance is \(\frac{220}{5}-6^2=8\), as required.

examples.title: Complete the variance square
examples.question: Add one real observation \(t\) to \(1,4,7\). Find the minimum possible descriptive variance and the value of \(t\) that gives it. Then find every real \(t\) for which the variance is at most \(6\).
solution: \[n_{\mathrm{new}}=4,\qquad T=12+t,\qquad Q=66+t^2.\]

\[V(t)=\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{16}(t-4)^2.\]

A real square is non-negative. The minimum is \(\frac{9}{2}\), attained only at \(t=4\).
\[V(t)\le6\Longleftrightarrow\frac{3}{16}(t-4)^2\le\frac{3}{2}\Longleftrightarrow(t-4)^2\le8.\]

\[-2\sqrt{2}\le t-4\le2\sqrt{2},\]\[4-2\sqrt{2}\le t\le4+2\sqrt{2}.\]

This includes both endpoints. A target variance below \(\frac{9}{2}\) would be impossible.

extraPractice.title: Replace the entry, not the whole dataset
extraPractice.prompt: Five lengths, in centimetres, have recorded mean \(6\) and recorded sum of squares \(220\). One entry of \(2\) should have been \(7\). Find the corrected count, mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: A replacement leaves the count unchanged. Recover the old total, then remove the incorrect value and its square before inserting the correct ones.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[n=5,\qquad T=5(6)=30,\qquad T_{\mathrm{new}}=30-2+7=35.\]
  2. \[Q_{\mathrm{new}}=220-2^2+7^2=265.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{35}{5}=7\ \text{cm},\qquad V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{265}{5}-7^2=4\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  4. \[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}=\sqrt{4}=2\ \text{cm}.\]

  5. The sum of squares changes by \(7^2-2^2=45\), not by \((7-2)^2=25\).

extraPractice.title: The same mean can accompany different spread
extraPractice.prompt: A list of five observations has total \(50\), sum of squares \(590\), and contains one observation equal to \(10\). Consider two separate changes to this original list: A removes that observation; B adds a new observation equal to \(10\). Find each new count and descriptive variance. How do the two new means compare with the original mean?

options.opposite: Removal decreases the mean and addition increases it.
options.equalspread: They remain equal because the variances are equal.

extraPractice.hint: Start again from the original list for each case. Update the count along with both totals. The value being added or removed equals the original mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{50}{5}=10,\qquad V=\frac{590}{5}-10^2=18.\]

  2. For A, remove exactly one record:

    \[n_A=4,\quad T_A=50-10=40,\quad Q_A=590-100=490.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}_A=10,\qquad V_A=\frac{490}{4}-10^2=\frac{45}{2}.\]

  4. For B, return to the original list and add a record:

    \[n_B=6,\quad T_B=60,\quad Q_B=690.\]
  5. \[\bar{x}_B=10,\qquad V_B=\frac{690}{6}-10^2=15.\]

  6. The mean stays the same in both cases. The sum of squared deviations from that unchanged mean remains \(90\), but its divisor changes from \(5\) to \(4\) or \(6\). Therefore the variances differ.

extraPractice.title: Remove only the extra copy
extraPractice.prompt: The recorded list is \(3,4,4,7,12\). An audit finds that one observation of \(4\) was accidentally entered twice. Remove only its extra copy. Find the corrected count, mean, median and descriptive standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: A duplicate is one extra record, not evidence that every occurrence of its value is wrong. Write the remaining ordered list before finding the median.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The corrected list is \(3,4,7,12\). It has \(n=4\), total \(T=26\), and sum of squares \(Q=218\).

  2. \[\bar{x}=\frac{26}{4}=\frac{13}{2},\qquad \text{median}=\frac{4+7}{2}=\frac{11}{2}.\]
  3. \[V=\frac{218}{4}-\left(\frac{13}{2}\right)^2=\frac{49}{4},\qquad \sigma=\frac{7}{2}.\]

  4. Removing both entries of \(4\) would delete a genuine observation as well as the extra copy.

extraPractice.title: Recover an ordered pair from two moments
extraPractice.prompt: The six observations \(1,4,6,9,p,q\) have mean \(6\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{32}{3}\). Given that \(p<q\), find the sum and sum of squares of the missing observations, then give the ordered pair \((p,q)\).
extraPractice.hint: Restore the full total and sum of squares first. Then use \((p+q)^2=p^2+q^2+2pq\) to form a quadratic with roots \(p\) and \(q\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T=6(6)=36,\qquad p+q=36-(1+4+6+9)=16.\]
  2. \[Q=6\left(\frac{32}{3}+6^2\right)=280,\qquad p^2+q^2=280-(1+16+36+81)=146.\]
  3. \[pq=\frac{16^2-146}{2}=55.\]
  4. \[z^2-16z+55=(z-5)(z-11)=0.\]

  5. The order condition selects \((p,q)=(5,11)\). The completed list has total \(36\) and sum of squares \(280\), which restore the stated mean and variance.

extraPractice.title: A positive proposed variance does not guarantee feasibility
extraPractice.prompt: A claim is made that the four real observations \(2,12,p,q\) have mean \(6\) and descriptive variance \(11\). Find the sum and sum of squares that \(p,q\) would need. Decide whether any real pair can satisfy the claim.

options.no: No: the two required moments contradict each other.
options.yes: Yes: every positive overall variance is possible.

extraPractice.hint: For any real pair, \((p-q)^2=2(p^2+q^2)-(p+q)^2\) must be non-negative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T=4(6)=24,\qquad p+q=24-(2+12)=10.\]
  2. \[Q=4(11+6^2)=188,\qquad p^2+q^2=188-(2^2+12^2)=40.\]
  3. \[(p-q)^2=2(40)-10^2=-20.\]

  4. A real square cannot be negative, so no real pair exists. Although the claimed whole-list variance is positive, it is incompatible with the two known observations. The repeated pair \(5,5\) has sum of squares \(50\), not \(40\).

starters.title: Recover the count before a correction and an addition
starters.question: A list of \(n\) masses, in grams, has recorded mean \(12\) and descriptive standard deviation \(2\). One recorded mass of \(8\) should have been \(20\). Correcting this entry increases the mean to \(13\). Find \(n\), the corrected sum of squares and the corrected standard deviation. Then a genuinely new observation of \(13\) g is added to the corrected list. Find its new descriptive variance.
starters.hint: The replacement changes the total by \(12\) but keeps \(n\) fixed. Use the change in mean to recover \(n\). Carry out the later addition only after completing the correction.
starters.solution:
1. \[12n-8+20=13n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=12.\]
  2. \[T_{\mathrm{old}}=144,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{old}}=12(2^2+12^2)=1776.\]
  3. \[T_{\mathrm{corrected}}=156,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{corrected}}=1776-8^2+20^2=2112.\]
  4. \[V_{\mathrm{corrected}}=\frac{2112}{12}-13^2=7\ \text{g}^{2},\qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{corrected}}=\sqrt{7}\ \text{g}.\]

  5. Now add the new record, increasing the count:

    \[n_{\mathrm{new}}=13,\quad T_{\mathrm{new}}=169,\quad Q_{\mathrm{new}}=2112+13^2=2281.\]
  6. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=13\ \text{g},\qquad V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{2281}{13}-13^2=\frac{84}{13}\ \text{g}^{2}.\]

  7. The mean remains \(13\) g. Its variance decreases from \(7\) because an extra observation at the mean adds zero squared deviation while increasing the divisor.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: relate the replacement to the change in mean.
  • 1 mark: recover the positive integer count.
  • 1 mark: reconstruct the original sum of squares using the squared SD.
  • 1 mark: update the sum of squares and obtain the corrected variance.
  • 1 mark: take the correct square root with units.
  • 1 mark: update the count and both totals for the later addition.
  • 1 mark: calculate the final variance and explain the unchanged mean.

starters.title: Use the whole variance condition, including restrictions
starters.question: Add a real observation \(t\) to \(2,5,8,11\). Let \(V(t)\) be the descriptive variance of all five observations. Find the minimum possible variance and the value of \(t\) attaining it. Find every real \(t\) for which \(V(t)=10\), and describe where \(V(t)\le10\). In a separate version, \(t\) must be a non-negative integer: list every allowed \(t\) with \(V(t)\le10\), then find the minimum variance under this integer restriction and every integer that attains it.
starters.hint: Use the new count of five and complete the square. A non-negative square identifies the real minimum; the nearest allowed integers to the centre identify the integer minimum.
starters.solution:
1. \[n=5,\qquad T=26+t,\qquad Q=214+t^2.\]
  2. \[V(t)=\frac{214+t^2}{5}-\left(\frac{26+t}{5}\right)^2=9+\frac{4}{25}\left(t-\frac{13}{2}\right)^2.\]

  3. The square is non-negative, so the real minimum is \(9\), attained only at \(t=\frac{13}{2}\).

  4. \[V(t)=10\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left(t-\frac{13}{2}\right)^2=\frac{25}{4}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t=4\ \text{or}\ t=9.\]
  5. \[V(t)\le10\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left|t-\frac{13}{2}\right|\le\frac{5}{2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad4\le t\le9.\]

  6. With the separate integer restriction, the complete allowed set is \(\{4,5,6,7,8,9\}\).

  7. The integers closest to \(\frac{13}{2}\) are \(6\) and \(7\), both a distance \(\frac{1}{2}\) away. Therefore

    \[V_{\mathrm{integer,min}}=9+\frac{4}{25}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{226}{25},\]

  8. attained at both \(t=6\) and \(t=7\). The unequal original observations prevent zero variance even when the extra value is optimally chosen.

• 1 mark: update the count, total and sum of squares.
  • 2 marks: derive the variance and complete the square correctly.
  • 1 mark: state the real minimum and where it occurs.
  • 1 mark: solve the equality with both branches.
  • 1 mark: obtain the closed interval for the inequality.
  • 1 mark: list every allowed integer.
  • 1 mark: identify both nearest integers to the real minimiser.
  • 1 mark: calculate the restricted minimum variance.

revision.body:
Track the count and both moment totals. Make the change before recalculating the summaries.

Recover the information behind the summaries

Let \(n\) be the count, \(T=\sum x\) the total and \(Q=\sum x^2\) the sum of squares.

\[T=n\bar{x},\qquad Q=n(V+\bar{x}^{\,2}),\qquad V=\frac{Q}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

Use descriptive variance \(V\) with divisor \(n>0\). SD is \(\sqrt{V}\); a supplied SD must be squared when restoring \(Q\).

Update exactly the records that changed

Replace \(a\) by \(b\): keep \(n\), use \(T-a+b\) and \(Q-a^2+b^2\). The sum of squares change is \(b^2-a^2\), not \((b-a)^2\).

Add \(t\): use \(n+1,\ T+t,\ Q+t^2\). Remove \(a\): use \(n-1,\ T-a,\ Q-a^2\), leaving at least one record. A duplicate means one extra copy: remove only that copy. Reorder the actual list to check a median.

Recover two missing observations

Subtract known records from the required totals to find \(s=p+q\) and \(r=p^2+q^2\). Then \(pq=\frac{s^2-r}{2}\), and the two missing values solve

\[z^2-sz+\frac{s^2-r}{2}=0.\]

Real values require \((p-q)^2=2r-s^2\ge0\). Keep every valid assignment, apply any order or context restriction, and restore both original moments. A mean alone usually leaves the pair undetermined.

Choose an additional real observation

Adding \(t\) to \(n\) records with mean \(\bar{x}\) and variance \(V\) gives

\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{nV}{n+1}+\frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(t-\bar{x})^2.\]

The real minimum is \(\frac{nV}{n+1}\), at \(t=\bar{x}\). Adding the old mean keeps the mean, reduces positive variance and leaves zero variance unchanged. Solve a target condition completely, then apply integer or range restrictions; they can change the minimum.
revision.checks:
• Replacement, addition or removal identified correctly?
  • Count and both totals updated in the right order?
  • All real branches and original restrictions checked?
  • Variance, SD, units and requested accuracy distinguished?
